paragraphs: October 26, 2004: Apple debuts the iPod Photo, a device capable of putting not just 15,000 songs in your pocket, but also 25,000 photographs. The new device “lets you take your entire music and photo library with you wherever you go,” Apple says.

It is the first iPod to offer a color screen and the ability to display digital images and album cover art. The iPod Photo represents a big step forward in the functionality of Apple’s iconic music player.

Before the iPhone turned the pocket-size screen into a window on your entire digital life, Apple experimented with what else its incredibly popular iPod music player could do. The iPod Photo upgraded the familiar monochrome display with a vivid color screen that could show album art, games and thousands of personal photos.

At the time, carrying your photo library around seemed like a luxury feature — and an expensive one, with prices starting at $499. But the bigger idea was unmistakably Apple: one portable device that brought more and more of your digital world along for the ride.

A fourth-generation iPod, the iPod Photo entered the product line at the height of the Apple music player’s cultural impact. And it brought innovative new features in addition to its 2-inch, 65,536-color LCD screen with LED backlight.

“iPod Photo holds up to 25,000 digital photos alongside your music library and displays them on its stunning high-resolution color screen, allowing you to scroll through your photo library almost instantly using iPod’s patent pending Click Wheel,” Apple said in a press release announcing the device. “iPod Photo lets you combine your music and your favorite photos to create magical slideshows on your iPod, and features TV-out for sharing your slideshows on big screen televisions and projectors.”

Improvements included increased playtime and the ability to send images to a television via composite-video or S-video cables. Beyond the screen and other updates, it retained the same Click Wheel controller as other iPods, along with then-standard FireWire and USB 2.0 connections.
The device came in two configurations: a 40GB model that retailed for $500 and a 60GB version that cost $600. This made the new device a relatively pricy (although tempting) proposition.
